ety.text: From Middle English hurten, hirten, hertan (“to injure, scathe, knock together”), from Old Northern French hurter ("to ram into, strike, collide with"; > Modern French heurter), perhaps from Frankish *hūrt (“a battering ram”), cognate with Welsh hwrdd (“ram”) and Cornish hordh (“ram”).

Unclear. Suggestions include: from its resemblance to a blue hurtleberry, or from French heurt (a blow, leaving a blue bruise), the latter of which would make it a doublet of hurt Etymology 1; compare the theories about golpe (“purple roundel”)).

senses.d: To cause (a person or animal) physical pain and/or injury.
ex: If anybody hurts my little brother, I will get upset.
This injection might hurt a little. Your arm will be hurting you for a while.

senses.d: To cause (somebody) emotional pain.
ex: He was deeply hurt he hadn’t been invited.

ex: Does your leg still hurt? / It is starting to feel better.

ety.text: Taíno *hurakābor. Spanish huracánbor. English hurricane Borrowed from Spanish huracán, ultimately from Taíno *hurakā.
Coined by Jeret Peterson.

senses.d: A severe tropical cyclone; an intense storm rotating around a central eye.
ex: Whole villages have been leveled by the hurricane coastal residents braced for.

senses.d: A severe tropical cyclone in the North Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, or in the eastern North Pacific off the west coast of Mexico, with winds of 119 km/h (74 miles per hour) or greater accompanied by rain, lightning, and thunder that sometimes moves into temperate latitudes.
ex: Near-synonyms: typhoon, cyclone
Janice was a tropical depression 10 days ago, a tropical storm 5 days ago, and a hurricane yesterday and today.

senses.d: A great forceful onrush.
A sweet alcoholic drink made with rum, lemon juice (or sometimes other fruit juice), and either passion fruit syrup or fassionola.
To be violent, with winds of 119 km/h (74 miles per hour) or greater, usually accompanied by rain, lightning, and thunder.
ex: Through the night it rained, hurricaned; sashes rattled; the chimney smoked; a lobby-door was ajar, and kept banging to and fro.
So I got inside my 'possum-skin—it hurricaned an' snowed— And I started for the Deepot, and lit out for his abode.

senses.d: To move noisily, quickly, and dramatically, becoming the center of attention.
ex: The Super nodded wisely, 'I agree, constable. See to it, Forbes!' and with that hurricaned out.
Angela Stripe was a force of nature. Bold and brave and brassy in a warm way, she never breezed in, she hurricaned.

senses.d: To attempt to accomplish a great deal with a frenzied effort.
To swirl quickly and violently.
ex: A whole swirl of turnarounds hurricaned from him.
Kona responded as air hurricaned out of the bay and water rushed in.

senses.d: To tear apart in a violent, destructive, and/or chaotic manner.
ex: Sharon gratefully assumed I'd hurricaned my last kitchen with my flour-tossing talents.
The other girls whispered to us 'He's hurricaning the room.'

senses.d: To cause an uproar.
ex: It blew open. It hurricaned onto shore.

senses.d: To storm excessivly; to fume and rage violently.
ex: He rang for the cook, and stormed and hurricaned and cycloned at her until the rain-clouds burst, and she wept.

senses.d: To chase violently or rush after and force along.
ex: As he hurricaned toward her, she turned and ran to the drop-off place.
Was there a sudden general strike, perhaps, sweeping up the doctors and nurses as it hurricaned upon them?

From Middle English horien (“to rush, impel”), probably a variation of hurren (“to vibrate rapidly, buzz”), from Proto-Germanic *hurzaną (“to rush”) (compare Middle High German hurren (“to hasten”), Norwegian hurre (“to whirl around”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”) (compare Latin currō (“to run”), Tocharian A kursär/Tocharian B kwarsär (“league; course”)). Related to hurr, horse, rush. Alternative etymology derives hurry as a variant of harry.

senses.d: A rushed action.
ex: Why are you in such a big hurry?

senses.d: An urgency.
ex: There is no hurry on that paperwork.

senses.d: An incidence of a defensive pressure that forces the quarterback to throw the ball earlier than intended or rush their decision, often leading to an incomplete pass or failed play.
A tremolando passage for violins, etc., accompanying an exciting situation.
To do things quickly.
ex: He's hurrying because he's late.

senses.d: Often with up, to speed up the rate of doing something.
ex: If you don't hurry (up) you won't finish on time.

senses.d: To cause to be done quickly.
To hasten; to impel to greater speed; to urge on.
ex: the rapid Stream presently draws him in , carries him away , and hurries him down violently.
They hurried him aboard a bark.

senses.d: To impel to precipitate or thoughtless action; to urge to confused or irregular activity.
ex: And wild amazement hurries up and down / The little number of your doubtful friends.

senses.d: To put: to convey coal in the mine, e.g. from the working to the tramway.
